node.label: Sarah Carter
node.date_label: Lost Harvests (1990) · Treaty 7 collective publication (1996) · Capturing Women (1997) · The Importance of Being Monogamous (2008) · Recollecting, co-edited (2011) · Imperial Plots (2016; corrected reprint 2018)
node.description: A historian of the Canadian Prairie West who links land, public policy, racial imagery and gender. In Lost Harvests she argues that many reserve residents sought agricultural livelihoods and that policies obstructed them, challenging an inherited explanation of cultural aversion. Capturing Women examines how constrained captivity narratives and racialized images helped police colonial boundaries. The Importance of Being Monogamous makes marriage a contested part of nation-building; Imperial Plots considers women’s unequal access to land alongside their participation in dispossession. Her selected bibliography also includes collective treaty research and co-editing, with those collaborative credits retained.

McCormack, 2011; metadata only); Imperial Plots (2016; introduction read in corrected reprint 2018).
node.scope_note: Reuses the existing sarah_carter identity and places her in historians. Read: Lost Harvests preface ix–x in the 2000 reprint; Capturing Women preface xiii–xvi; The Importance of Being Monogamous imprint and pp. 3–9; Imperial Plots imprint and introduction pp. 3–11, 19–23 in the corrected 2018 reprint; and the English written interview published online in 2021. Complete monographs remain unread. Collective authorship of Treaty 7 and Carter/McCormack’s co-editorship of Recollecting are bibliographic facts, without attributing others’ testimony or chapters to Carter. Earlier source notes and collective field comparisons retain their IDs and qualifications. A specific later reading of Imperial Plots does not retrospectively identify Lost Harvests as an adoption of Wolfe’s theory. Research on Indigenous history and a Native Studies appointment establish no Indigenous identity. No career interval or comprehensive later-work review is asserted.

people_update.identity_note: Historian of the Canadian Prairie West, identified by the primary book imprints and publisher/institutional author biographies as the author of Lost Harvests, Capturing Women and Imperial Plots. Existing graph identity reused; no merger with namesakes and no authority QID assigned. Research subject and Native Studies affiliation do not establish Indigenous identity.

proposed_edges.relationship: Recasts reserve agriculture as a history of Indigenous initiatives and government constraints rather than an assumed cultural rejection of farming (Lost Harvests, 1990).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary preface ix–x, read in the reprint marked 2000, retaining the 1990 publication. Carter describes a change in her own initial hypothesis after examining sources; her claim concerns many, not all, reserve residents. This arrow records her historical interpretation, not independent verification of the unread chapters. Collective regional/encounter comparisons edge_809 and edge_869 retain their original IDs and endpoints.

proposed_edges.relationship: Joins racial imagery and the regulation of marriage to the history of women’s unequal options and colonial nation-building in the Prairie West (1997; 2008).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Capturing Women, complete preface xiii–xvi, and The Importance of Being Monogamous, opening pp. 3–9, read. These are different investigations: constrained public representations and the imposition/contestation of marital norms. The latter also states limits to state power and the persistence of Indigenous marriage law. The arrow does not substitute the publisher summary for a whole-book reading or give one experience to all women.

proposed_edges.relationship: Examines how British women’s struggles for prairie land combined gendered exclusion with unequal participation in Indigenous dispossession (Imperial Plots, 2016; read in corrected reprint 2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read introduction pp. 3–11, 19–23. P. 6 explicitly engages Wolfe, while pp. 9–10 qualify settler women’s privileges and complicity; the later pages explain cross-border and imperial scales. The source now exceeds the prior publisher-page-only evidence, whose wording and date remain in its verification history. This contribution concerns this specific later work; it neither assigns her entire earlier bibliography to one paradigm nor asserts an influence relationship from the citation alone.

screq_carter_1990.note: Primary preface ix–x, title/imprint and contents now read in the publisher-distributor preview https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9780773562431_A23655373/preview-9780773562431_A23655373.pdf. This is the reprint marked 2000, retaining copyright/legal deposit 1990 and first paperback 1993, not a newly published book in 2000. Carter explains that source research changed her initial cultural-aversion hypothesis and argues that many, not all, reserve residents sought farming while policy and later land surrender obstructed it. The rest of the monograph, including the agricultural-policy chapters, remains unread. This bounded primary reading supplements rather than erases the earlier metadata-only witness or its pre-paradigm chronology qualification.

screq_carter_2008.note: Title/imprint and opening chapter pp. 3–9 now read in the publisher’s OA first-edition PDF, also archived by Library and Archives Canada: https://epe.lac-bac.gc.ca/100/200/300/athabasca_univ/importance_being/Sarah_Carter.pdf?nodisclaimer=1 . Imprint explicitly identifies University of Alberta Press AND AU Press, Athabasca University, first edition/first printing 2008. Title is “to 1915”; the current AU landing-page heading’s “in 1915” is not copied. The read opening connects marriage, gender and nation-building while stating that state power was limited/contested and Indigenous marriage/divorce law persisted. Remaining chapters and the later conclusion unread; no wholesale verification of the book or its quoted historical sources.

p4b_carter_2016.note: Publisher OA copy now consulted through https://escholarship.umanitoba.ca/projects/imperial-plots : title/imprint plus introduction pp. 3–11 and 19–23 read. This copy explicitly says copyright 2016, “Reprinted with corrections 2018”; first-printing text not collated. P. 6 expressly cites Patrick Wolfe’s elimination argument; pp. 9–10 discuss reproduction and women’s uneven privileges/complicity, and pp. 19–20 describe transnational and imperial scales. This updates the earlier publisher-page-only observation: the book’s read introduction does engage settler-colonial arguments, although that phrase was absent from the publisher description. No general attribution of her earlier work to Wolfe follows. Rest of the book unread; source-specific claims are attributed to the corrected reprint actually consulted.

row.context: Studies racial imagery, marriage and land as related but distinct ways that gender and colonial power were made and contested in the Prairie West. Her selected openings preserve differences among women’s positions and limits to state control.
